opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it is just that benchmarks are so convenient. You write down a set of tasks, you run the model, you get a number, and you can put that number in a chart next to every other model. It's cheap, it's repeatable, and it fits the way the ML research community already works. The whole field grew up around shared leaderboards like ImageNet, so there's a lot of cultural momentum behind "make a dataset, report a score."

The other kinds of evidence I care about are messier. That includes things like randomized controlled trials where you give some people AI assistance and not others and see how their productivity changes. It includes surveys of how people are actually using these systems at work, field studies inside companies, and even really careful anecdotes from expert users. Those are slow and expensive. They're noisy and hard to standardize. By the time a six-month study comes out, two new model generations have shipped, so people feel the results are stale before they're published. And they don't produce a clean number you can track over time the way a benchmark does.

There's also a skill-set mismatch. Running an RCT on knowledge workers looks more like economics or social science than machine learning. The people best positioned to build evals are ML engineers, and they reach for the tools they know.

But I think that's a real problem, because benchmarks have gotten systematically worse at telling us what we actually want to know. They saturate quickly. They're often contaminated or over-optimized. And above all, they're made of self-contained, well-specified tasks with clear right answers, which is exactly the regime where AI looks most impressive. Real work is full of ambiguity, long time horizons, messy context and coordination with other people. So you can have a model that crushes a benchmark and then find it only gives modest speedups in the real world. Sometimes it even slows experienced people down, which a few studies have found.

If the question we care about is "how much is AI changing the world, and how fast?", then at some point you have to go measure the world. Benchmarks are a leading indicator, but they're a proxy, and I'd like to see a lot more investment in the slower, more expensive evidence that tells us whether the proxy is tracking reality.

r001.rationale: It says non-benchmark evidence is slow, expensive, noisy, hard to standardize, and lacks a clean trackable number, explaining why benchmarks are more convenient and attract more interest.

r002.rationale: It says benchmark scores can coexist with modest real-world speedups and sometimes slower work, but does not claim benchmarks consistently overestimate real-world performance.

r003.rationale: It links the challenge of measuring real-world performance to ambiguity, long time horizons, messy context, and coordination in real work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few reasons, and some of them are pretty reasonable and some of them I think are kind of unfortunate.

The reasonable part is that benchmarks are legible. If I tell you a model gets 85% on some coding benchmark and the last one got 60%, you can put that on a chart, you can compare across labs, you can track it over time. It's quantitative, it's reproducible, somebody else can run the same test and check your number. That's really valuable, and I don't want to dismiss it. A lot of the other evidence we could look at, like how people are actually using these systems at work, or what tasks they're delegating and how often they're satisfied with the result, is messy. It's anecdotal, it's confounded by who's using it and what they're using it for, and it's hard to turn into a single number that moves up and to the right.

But I think the less-good reason is that benchmarks are what the field was already set up to produce. Machine learning as an academic discipline grew up around leaderboards. You propose a method, you beat the state of the art on a dataset, you publish. So when the question shifted from "is this architecture better than that one" to "how capable are these systems, really, in a way that matters for the world," people kind of reached for the tool they already had. And that tool is good at answering the first question and not that great at answering the second.

The thing I keep coming back to is that benchmarks measure what's easy to measure, not necessarily what we care about. We care about things like, can this system do a week of a junior engineer's job without someone checking in? Can it run an experiment end to end? Can it notice when it's confused and stop? Those are really hard to benchmark because they're long-horizon, they involve a lot of context, and the "right answer" is often ambiguous. So we end up with a lot of short, self-contained problems with clean grading, and then we're surprised when a model saturates those and still can't do the thing we actually wanted.

And there's a dynamic where once a benchmark becomes a target, it stops being a good measurement. Labs train on things that look like it, contamination creeps in, and the number keeps going up while your sense of what the number means gets fuzzier. So I actually think things like uplift studies, where you give people the tool and see what happens to their productivity, or just carefully looking at deployment data about what tasks are getting automated, are underrated. They're noisier, but they're closer to the question we're asking. I'd like to see the field put a lot more effort into making that kind of evidence rigorous instead of treating it as a footnote to the leaderboard.

r001.rationale: The response says real-world usage evidence is messy, confounded, and hard to reduce to a single number, making it harder to measure than benchmarks.

r002.rationale: It says benchmarks can saturate while models still struggle with desired tasks and that benchmark scores can become less meaningful, but does not state that benchmarks consistently overestimate real-world performance.

r003.rationale: It attributes the difficulty of benchmarking relevant capabilities to tasks being long-horizon, context-heavy, and often lacking an unambiguous right answer.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is that benchmarks are just much easier to work with. You have a number, you can compare it across models, and you can see whether it went up. That’s useful if you’re a researcher trying to demonstrate progress, and it’s useful if you’re trying to communicate that progress to other people.

Other kinds of evidence are often messier. If you watch a model try to carry out a long task, it might do something really impressive and then make a very basic mistake. How do you summarize that? And how much of the outcome was about the model versus the instructions it got, the tools it had, or how much help someone gave it? It takes more judgment to interpret that evidence, and people can disagree about what it means.

So I think there’s a tendency to focus on what’s easy to measure and compare. The concern is that the things we ultimately care about—whether an AI can reliably do useful work, for example—aren’t necessarily captured very well by those measurements. Benchmarks are evidence, but I wouldn’t want them to be the only evidence we look at.

r001.rationale: The response says non-benchmark evidence is messier to summarize and interpret, which makes it harder to use and compare.

r002.rationale: It does not say benchmarks consistently overestimate real-world performance.

r003.rationale: It mentions long tasks and interpretation challenges, but does not attribute measurement difficulty to the open-ended nature of the real world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is that benchmarks are very convenient. You get a number, you can compare it to another number, and you can track progress over time. Whereas if somebody says, “I spent a week trying to get this model to do my job, and here’s what happened,” that can be very informative, but it’s harder to know how much to generalize. How good were they at prompting? How representative was the work? How much help did they give the model?

And I think there’s a real coordination advantage to benchmarks. If everybody evaluates on the same thing, you have a shared reference point. With other kinds of evidence, you often need to spend a lot more time understanding the context before you can interpret the result.

But that convenience can also be misleading. The thing we ultimately care about is what these systems can actually do in the world. So I’d like to see more careful, detailed attempts to use them for consequential tasks, even if the results are harder to summarize in a single number.

r001.rationale: The response says non-benchmark results are harder to generalize and interpret, but it does not attribute lower interest to difficulty devising good non-benchmark measures.

r002.rationale: It says benchmark convenience can be misleading, but does not state that benchmarks consistently overestimate real-world performance.

r003.rationale: It notes that consequential-task results are harder to summarize, but does not attribute measurement difficulty to the open-ended nature of the real world.
